name: driverkit
description: Make a web app drivable by an agent. No pixels, no selectors, no model.
//exports: One install, one version, one changelog. The five areas are subpaths rather
than packages because the library's contract is one function -- `mount()` --
and six package.jsons for one function is a table of contents pretending to
be an architecture. Tree-shaking keeps a page free of what it does not import;
`sideEffects: false` below is what lets a bundler prove that.
`./relay` is the one entry that is NOT browser-safe: it imports `node:http`,
which is what drove the original split in the first place. It is published
under a `node` condition and NOTHING else, so a browser-targeted resolver
finds no target for the subpath and fails loudly at build time, rather than
pulling `node:http` into a page bundle and failing at runtime. There is
deliberately no `browser` or `default` fallback: a shim that resolved to an
empty module would hand somebody a `createRelay` that silently does nothing.
See `test/packaging.test.ts`, which resolves every subpath under browser
conditions and asserts this one is unreachable.
The same strictness reaches TypeScript, and it is worth knowing before it
surprises somebody: `moduleResolution: "bundler"` applies the conditions a
bundler applies, so `import { createRelay } from "driverkit/relay"` is a
TS2307 under it -- correctly, since that code could not have been bundled
either. Server code that imports the relay wants `moduleResolution:
"nodenext"`, under which every subpath here resolves.
//dependencies: `@types/node` is a real dependency and not a dev one: dist/relay/relay.d.ts and
dist/relay/serve.d.ts both re-export `node:http` types in their PUBLIC surface, so a
consumer who installs driverkit without it gets TS2307 on the package's own
declarations the moment they import `driverkit/relay`. A types package in
`dependencies` is the documented answer to exactly that case. It is the price of
shipping the relay in the same package as the browser code; nothing is emitted
into a page bundle by a types-only dependency.
//peerDependencies: `./react` is a second, optional panel for a host that already has React; the
vanilla `./widget` is hand-written DOM and still depends on nothing. Somebody who
installs driverkit and never imports `driverkit/react` must not get React in their
lockfile and must not get an unresolvable import in the .d.ts files this package
publishes, and FOUR things have to hold for that, of which this field is one:
1. `optional: true` below, so npm neither installs React nor warns about a peer
somebody correctly does not have. `>=18` because `useSyncExternalStore` is an
18 API and it is the one that makes that area small.
2. React is in no `dependencies`. The one dependency is still `@types/node`.
3. NO FILE IN THE PACKAGE IMPORTS `react`, in any form, `import type` included.
This is the part peer-optional does not buy: `import type { ReactNode } from
"react"` in a published .d.ts is a dangling module reference for every
consumer who did not install React. There is nothing to dangle because the
React API is typed STRUCTURALLY in src/react/runtime.ts and handed in --
`createDriverPanel(React)` -- which is also how a host is kept from ever
rendering our components against a second copy of React's hook dispatcher.
Same reasoning, and the same shape, as `./otel` taking a `Tracer`.
4. Nothing in core, agent, widget, controls, browser, check, otel or relay
imports that area, so it is not in the module graph of somebody importing
only `driverkit`.
All four are asserted in test/packaging.test.ts, including that the emitted
JavaScript under dist/react names no bare specifier at all -- not even `react`.
